scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Salegy originated in the 1950s in northwestern Madagascar as an electrified form of the traditional antsa music performed by Betsimisaraka and Tsimihety peoples during possession rituals.
It evolved from Sub-Saharan African folk roots and was modernized with electric guitars and synthesizers.
Eusèbe Jaojoby, a Sakalava singer, was a key figure in popularizing salegy internationally.
on_screen: Map: Madagascar · Africa

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Salegy is performed at social celebrations, nightclubs, and parties throughout Madagascar.
It derives from ritual music used in possession rites to invoke spirits but today is a popular dance music form symbolizing Malagasy identity and communal joy.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Salegy music features ringing electric guitars with high-life style lines, real or synthesized accordion, heavy electric bass, and a percussion section including a Western drum kit, djembe, and shakers.
The rhythm is syncopated and polyrhythmic in 6/8 or 12/4 time with accents on the 3rd or 7th beat, typically around 290 BPM.
Listen for the electric guitar, accordion (real or synthesized), electric bass, drum kit.
The pulse is 6/8 or 12/4.

Salegy features fast, ringing electric guitars with high-life melodies, layered with synthesized accordion lines and heavy bass. The percussion drives a rapid, syncopated polyrhythm with djembe and drum kit accents, while polyphonic vocals engage in call-and-response, creating an energetic and danceable soundscape.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Eusèbe Jaojoby is known as the 'King of Salegy' and a pioneer of the genre.
Other important artists include Ninie Doniah, Vaiavy Chila, Dr. J.B. and the Jaguars, Wawa, and Aly Mourad.

Salegy is part of a family of northern Malagasy musical styles including tsapiky (south), basesa (east), goma (north), kawitry (north), malesa (northwest), antosy (northwest), bahoejy (northwest), salesa (northwest), alalaosy (northwest), mgodro (Mayotte), and salegue (La Réunion).
Salegy descends from the traditional antsa music of Betsimisaraka and Tsimihety peoples, itself rooted in Sub-Saharan African folk traditions.

scenes.title: Family tree

Salegy is regional variant of tsapiky: Southern Malagasy dance music related to salegy.
Salegy is regional variant of basesa: Eastern Malagasy dance music with stylistic links.
Salegy is regional variant of goma: Northern Malagasy style related to salegy.
